original_question: If C is a compact subset of [0, infinity) containing 0, does there exist a compact set K subset R whose center of distances C(K) is exactly C?
target_in_paper: Conjecture 1.1 in Section 1: the compact realizability problem for centers of distances.
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the main mathematical core of the paper-faithful target: a compact set C contained in [0, infinity) with 0 in C, and the question whether there exists a compact set K in the real line whose center of distances is exactly C. It also correctly asks for exact realization, not merely inclusion or approximation.
missing_details: The paper’s notation for the center of distances is S(K), not C(K).
The center of distances should be defined explicitly: S(K) = {t in [0, infinity) : for every x in K there exists y in K with |x-y| = t}.
The ambient metric is the usual Euclidean metric on the real line, so distances are absolute differences |x-y|.
The quantified distance parameter t is restricted to nonnegative reals.
To make the question fully stand-alone, one should state that equality S(K) = C is required exactly, not up to closure or inclusion.

The nearby context in the paper matters: Proposition 1.2 gives a weaker positive result with a closed (not necessarily compact) realizing set, and Theorem 1.3 gives a realization by a Bernstein set; this shows the intended target is specifically the compact version, not the broader realizability problem.
refined_question: Let C be a compact subset of [0, infinity) with 0 in C. Does there exist a compact set K subset of R such that S(K) = C, where S(K) := {t in [0, infinity) : for every x in K there exists y in K with |x-y| = t} is the center of distances of K (with respect to the usual metric on R)?
justification: The draft is aiming at the paper’s Section 1 compact-realization question, which is presented as Conjecture 1.1. The surrounding context confirms this exact scope: Proposition 1.2 records a weaker realization theorem using a closed subset of [0, infinity), and Theorem 1.3 records a different realization theorem using a Bernstein subset of R. That nearby progression shows that the intended open problem is specifically whether compact data C can be realized by a compact K, not the broader question of realization by an arbitrary or merely closed set.
